 New England governors seek more money for heating aid 
 The bipartisan group of governors, including Gov. Ned Lamont (D), is worried the LIHEAP program won't have enough funding to get through the winter.   
 By Mike Savino • 
 Published November 10, 2026 • 
 Updated on November 10, 2026 at 6:23 pm 
 BOOKMARKER 
 NBC Universal, Inc. 
 Connecticut families are facing rising home heating costs as colder weather approaches, prompting concerns about whether enough funding is available for heating assistance.
 All six New England governors are asking Congress to put an additional $3 billion into the Low-Income Heating Assistance Program.  
 The bipartisan group of governors, including Gov. Ned Lamont (D), is worried the LIHEAP program won't have enough funding to get through the winter.

 In the letter, the governors expressed concern that heating oil prices could be 50% higher than they were last year.  
 Lamont also told reporters during an event in North Haven that Connecticut has seen a 12% increase in applications for help.  
 "Obviously applications are up," Lamont said. "Because of the war in Iran, the high price of heating of your home."  
 David Perzan, of New Britain, said he wants to see the federal government take steps to bring down fuel costs.  
 "It affects everybody tremendously, dramatically," he said. "Everybody's hurting. It's a domino effect."

 Joy Allen, also of New Britain, said she has had to rely on assistance from the Connecticut Energy Assistance Program, or CEAP, the state's version.  
 She said she wouldn't be able to make ends meet if the program ran out of money.  
 "This program is very beneficial to people, so I would hope they don't run out of funds to help people because it is, you know – it helps people," Allen said.  
 United Way of Connecticut President and CEO Lisa Tepper Bates said her organization's helpline saw calls more than double from people seeking information on assistance.  
 She also said many of the people told United Way they were putting off buying oil as long as possible, hoping the prices would come down.  
 "A lot of families are looking at the cold temperatures thinking about what just one tank of heating fuel will cost them," Tepper Bates said.  
 She called on the state to increase the income caps for eligibility.  
 A single person cannot earn more than $48,714 to qualify for assistance. That cap rises to $93,681 for a family of four.  
 United Way of Connecticut conducts an annual report on people considered asset-limited, income-constrained and employed, or ALICE, a grouping of people who earn too much to qualify for assistance programs but still struggle to pay their bills.  
 Tepper Bates said that a family of four would need to earn roughly $116,000 to survive, leaving a gap of more than $20,000 between the LIHEAP income gap and the amount United Way of Connecticut considers a living wage.  
 "So we do worry that there are a lot of families that are struggling and are not going to covered by the program under the current parameters," he said. 
 Lamont has already utilized $12.7 million from an emergency fund to help bolster the amount of assistance available.  
 He told reporters Tuesday he's open to doing more, including raising the income caps.  
 "I know we have to do more," he said. "But as I always warn people, I can't make up for all the cuts coming out of Washington, but I'm going to take care of the most vulnerable." 
 U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA) and Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-SD) did not respond to requests for comment on whether they support additional funding.  
 Congress will need to approve a funding bill by Dec. 11 to avoid a partial shutdown of the federal government.
